chapters.title: 9.1 Cross-Origin Testing (cy.origin())
chapters.overviewText: Cypress test code shares a JavaScript realm with the app iframe, so the browser's same-origin policy is a hard wall — not a Cypress bug. cy.origin(url, { args }, callback) re-injects a serialized callback into the third-party origin. Outer-scope variables are invisible inside that callback; pass JSON-serializable data via args, and yield/return values back to the primary origin.
chapters.why: SSO (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace) is the most common production reason Cypress tests die after a redirect. Interviewers distinguish people who can draw cy.origin's args/return contract from people who only remember chromeWebSecurity: false.
chapters.when: Any flow that leaves app.bizlevate.com — IdP login, payment widget, help-center iframe on another host, OAuth consent. Write this chapter before stubbing SSO out of existence.

practical.scenario: Employee login redirects to login.okta.com, then back to /dashboard with a session cookie.
practical.pass: You wrap Okta steps in cy.origin('https://login.okta.com', { args: creds }, ({ username, password }) => { ... }) and yield a value back if the primary origin needs it. You do not close over outer variables.
practical.fail: You type into #username after the redirect with no cy.origin, or you reference `password` from the outer test inside the origin callback.

chapters.customSummary:
- cy.origin(url, callback) or cy.origin(url, { args }, callback) — callback is serialized into the other origin; it cannot close over outer locals.
- args must be JSON/structured-clone serializable (strings, numbers, plain objects/arrays) — no functions, DOM nodes, or class instances.
- The callback's yielded/returned value becomes the new subject on the primary origin — that is how you get data back.
- Cypress.require() (or commands registered for that origin) is how custom commands become available inside the callback.
- Playwright navigates cross-origin with no extra API. Selenium is an external driver so SOP never bound the test process. chromeWebSecurity: false is a last-resort anti-pattern, not the lesson.

chapters.title: 9.2 Working Around Cypress's Architectural Limits
chapters.overviewText: Every famous Cypress limitation — cross-origin, multi-tab, one browser per run, no first-class WebKit, no in-process parallel browsers — is a consequence of 'the test lives in the page,' not a missing checkbox on the roadmap. Senior work is matching the limitation to a substitute (origin block, cy.request, href assertion, separate suite in Playwright) instead of fighting the iframe.
chapters.why: Teams waste months trying to make Cypress behave like an external driver. Knowing which walls are architectural keeps Bizlevate's suite honest and keeps interview answers from sounding like tool tribalism.
chapters.when: When a ticket says 'also assert the PDF tab' or 'login is on another domain,' before writing a plugin. Revisit when flake traces back to chromeWebSecurity or a target=_blank click.

practical.scenario: A product manager wants one Cypress spec to: log in via Okta, open a payslip PDF in a new tab, and compare two employees side by side.
practical.pass: You split the work: cy.origin for Okta, cy.request or href checks for the PDF, and you say the side-by-side tab requires Playwright (or two sequential visits). You do not promise cy.switchToTab().
practical.fail: You disable web security, add cy.wait(5000), and claim Cypress will 'soon' do multi-tab because Playwright does.

chapters.customSummary:
- In-page architecture ⇒ same-origin wall, one privileged iframe at a time, no two live tab DOMs.
- Substitutes: cy.origin, cy.request, assert href/target, stub window.open, visit the URL in the same tab.
- chromeWebSecurity: false and 'just use Electron' are not architecture workarounds.
- Playwright/Selenium win when the product's critical path is multi-tab, Safari/WebKit, or non-JS bindings.
- Choosing Playwright for one suite is a senior call, not a Cypress failure.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## The constraint, restated mechanically

Cypress owns one browser, one runner page, one app iframe, one command queue. Privileged access is into *that* iframe's JavaScript realm. Anything that would require the test process to hold two page handles at once (two tabs, two unrelated origins without `cy.origin`, a native WebView) is outside the model.

Selenium's `switchTo().window(handle)` and Playwright's `Page` objects exist because those tools are external observers. Asking Cypress for the same API is asking it to stop being Cypress.

## A substitution table you can actually use

| Product behavior | Cypress substitute | When the substitute is not enough |
|---|---|---|
| Redirect through Okta | `cy.origin` (9.1) | IdP uses a popup + opener messaging you cannot observe |
| `target="_blank"` payslip | Assert `href` + `target`, or `cy.request(href)` | You must *read rendered PDF pixels in the new tab* |
| `window.open` compare-employees | Stub `window.open`, then `cy.visit` the URL | Two live DOMs must stay open and interact |
| Third-party chat widget iframe | `cy.origin` or isolate it out of E2E | Closed shadow + cross-origin + popup together |
| Safari/iOS web-view bug | Do not pretend: no first-class WebKit | That bug is the test's reason to exist |
| Native iOS/Android HRM app | Out of scope — Appium | Always |

## Patterns that look like workarounds but are not

**Sleep.** `cy.wait(8000)` after an SSO redirect does not restore privileged access.

**`chromeWebSecurity: false`.** Turns off a browser guarantee. Breaks Firefox parity. Hides real product bugs (mixed content, CORS).

**Conditional `if (Cypress.$('okta-form').length)`.** You are querying the *old* origin's DOM. The Okta form is not there.

**Electron-only CI.** Electron is bundled Chromium, not "all browsers." It does not fix origin or tabs.

## The senior decision

If a large fraction of Bizlevate's *revenue-critical* journeys are multi-tab document compare, Safari-only bugs, or popup OAuth, put *those* journeys in Playwright (or Selenium, if the org is already there). Keep Cypress for in-app HRM journeys and component tests. That split is cheaper than a year of origin-callback archaeology.

Interview line: "I don't work around architecture with sleeps. I substitute (`cy.origin`, `cy.request`, href) or I change tools for that path."

chapters.title: 9.3 Multi-Tab / New Window Limitations & Workarounds
chapters.overviewText: There is no cy.switchToTab(), no Page-object handle for a second window, and no supported way to drive two live tab DOMs in one Cypress test. target=_blank and window.open still happen at the OS level in headed mode — Cypress simply cannot address the new document. Workarounds verify intent (href/target), fetch the resource with cy.request, stub window.open, or visit the URL in the same tab.
chapters.why: Payslips, tax forms, and 'open in new tab' help articles are everywhere in HRM. Interviewers use 'how do you test a PDF that opens in a new tab' to see if you know the architectural ceiling.
chapters.when: Any click that sets target=_blank, calls window.open, or uses rel=noopener. Design the assertion before you write the click.

practical.scenario: On the compensation page, View Payslip opens /api/payslips/42.pdf in a new tab. You must prove the employee gets the right document.
practical.pass: You assert the link href and target, then cy.request the href with the session cookie and check status/content-type/body. You never call switchToTab.
practical.fail: You look for cy.switchToWindow() or copy a Selenium window-handle loop into a Cypress spec.

chapters.customSummary:
- There is no cy.switchToTab() / switchToWindow() — that API does not exist because Cypress has one privileged iframe.
- Headed runs may visually open a second tab; the command log still talks to the original tab.
- Substitutes: assert href+target, cy.request the URL, stub window.open, strip target and cy.visit in-tab.
- Playwright: page.waitForEvent('popup') / context.new_page(). Selenium: window handles + switchTo().window.
- If the test's job is two live DOMs interacting, that test belongs in Playwright.

chapters.title: 9.4 Shadow DOM Support
chapters.overviewText: Open Shadow DOM is reachable in Cypress only when you opt in: per-query .shadow() or the global/test includeShadowDom flag. Closed shadow roots stay closed — no test tool gets a free pass. Playwright pierces open shadow trees by default; Selenium requires getShadowRoot() / ShadowRoot.cy.
chapters.why: Design-system buttons, date pickers, and third-party web components hide their internals in shadow trees. A cy.get('.inner-label') that works in DevTools-on-the-flattened-tree will timeout in Cypress until you pierce.
chapters.when: Any control implemented as a custom element (leave-type dropdown, file chip, design-system Modal). Also when a test 'sees' an element in the browser but Cypress reports 0 matches.

practical.scenario: The Leave Type control is <hrm-select> with an open shadow root containing input.native-input. You must type 'Annual' and choose the option.
practical.pass: You use cy.get('hrm-select').shadow().find('input.native-input') or set includeShadowDom: true for that get, then type and assert.
practical.fail: You cy.get('input.native-input') as if the shadow tree were a normal descendant, or you assume Playwright-style automatic piercing.

chapters.customSummary:
- Default Cypress queries do not cross shadow boundaries.
- Pierce with .shadow() on a host, or includeShadowDom: true (config, cy.get options, or Cypress.config).
- Closed mode shadow roots are not queryable — test via published API, slots, or accessibility tree, not internals.
- Playwright: open shadow pierced by default. Selenium: explicit getShadowRoot().
- Prefer page objects that encapsulate the host + shadow find so specs do not leak internals.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## The default that surprises people

```js
cy.get('input.native-input'); // 0 matches — it lives under <hrm-select>'s shadow root
```

Light DOM `querySelector` does not enter shadow trees. Cypress uses that same model unless you opt in. Playwright's locator engine *does* pierce open shadow DOM by default, which is why a copied Playwright selector can fail in Cypress even when "the element is obviously there."

## Per-element pierce

```js
cy.get('[data-cy=leave-type-host]')
  .shadow()
  .find('input.native-input')
  .type('Annual{enter}');
```

`.shadow()` yields the shadow root of the current subject (must be a host element). Then `.find()` / `.contains()` run inside that root.

## Opt-in globally or per command

```js
// cypress.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: { includeShadowDom: true },
});

// or one query
cy.get('hrm-select', { includeShadowDom: true })
  .find('input.native-input')
  .type('Annual');
```

Global `includeShadowDom: true` is convenient for a design-system-heavy HRM. It also makes selectors more expensive and can match *through* components you did not intend. Prefer host-then-`.shadow()` in shared commands (`cy.getLeaveType()` ) so the pierce is named.

## Closed shadow roots

If the component was created with `{ mode: 'closed' }`, neither Cypress, Playwright, nor honest Selenium tests should scrape internals. Drive it like a user: slots, visible text, `data-cy` on the host, or the component's public events. If you cannot, that is a testability bug in the component, not a Cypress gap.

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

| | Cypress | Playwright | Selenium 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open shadow | Opt-in (`.shadow()` / `includeShadowDom`) | Pierced by default | `element.getShadowRoot()` then find |
| Closed shadow | No | No (by design) | No |
| Nested shadows | Chain `.shadow()` | Locator still pierces open trees | Chain getShadowRoot |

Interview line: "Cypress does not pierce shadow by default. I `.shadow()` from the host or set `includeShadowDom`. Closed roots stay a contract with the component, not a locator problem."

chapters.title: 9.5 Component Testing (Cypress CT)
chapters.overviewText: Cypress Component Testing mounts one component with cy.mount() into a real browser page — same cy.get/click/type as E2E, no running HRM server, router, or database. A separate component: {} config block and specs that live next to the component are the convention. CT answers 'does this piece work given these props?'; E2E answers 'does the integrated product work?' Neither replaces the other.
chapters.why: LeaveRequestForm edge cases (zero balance, 500-row cost centers, disabled submit) are expensive as E2E and cheap as CT. Interviewers want that distinction, plus the fact that Playwright CT exists but is less central, and Selenium has no equivalent.
chapters.when: When building or refactoring a React/Vue/Angular component with meaningful UI states. Not as a substitute for login→submit→approve journeys.

practical.scenario: You must cover LeaveRequestForm: empty, valid Annual leave, remainingBalance=0, and that onSubmit receives the right payload — without seeding payroll data.
practical.pass: You add a component config, colocate LeaveRequestForm.cy.tsx, cy.mount(<LeaveRequestForm ... />), stub onSubmit, and keep one E2E for the real submit/approve path.
practical.fail: You only write E2E for every prop combination, or you claim CT makes E2E unnecessary.

chapters.customSummary:
- cy.mount(component) renders isolated UI in a real browser with the same commands as E2E.
- e2e and component are separate config blocks (devServer framework + bundler).
- Specs conventionally sit beside the component, not only under cypress/e2e.
- CT ≠ E2E: isolation and speed vs real routing, APIs, and cross-page state.
- Playwright has component testing later/less central; Selenium has none — this is a Cypress strong suit.

chapters.title: 9.6 Visual Regression Testing
chapters.overviewText: Cypress has no built-in visual diff API. cy.screenshot() captures pixels; it does not compare them. Visual regression is always a plugin (cypress-image-snapshot and similar) or a paid SaaS (Percy, Applitools, Chromatic). Playwright ships expect(page).to_have_screenshot() / toHaveScreenshot() as first-party. Selenium has nothing built-in either.
chapters.why: Dashboard and payslip layout regressions are real HRM bugs. Claiming 'Cypress does visual testing' in an interview is false unless you name the add-on. Knowing the free vs paid split prevents a surprise procurement conversation.
chapters.when: When pixel layout of a page or component is a requirement, or when a designer asks for screenshot diffs in PRs. Not as a substitute for role/permission assertions.

practical.scenario: A CSS change shifts the payroll summary cards by 8px. You want CI to fail before employees see a broken dashboard.
practical.pass: You say Cypress has no built-in visual matcher, add cypress-image-snapshot or Percy, commit baselines, and review diffs. You do not treat cy.screenshot() as a comparison.
practical.fail: You call cy.screenshot() and assume the next run will fail on pixel drift, or you say Cypress includes Playwright-style toHaveScreenshot.

chapters.customSummary:
- No first-party visual matcher in Cypress — unlike Playwright's toHaveScreenshot.
- cy.screenshot() is capture (and CI artifact), not regression.
- Free path: cypress-image-snapshot (pixel diff, baselines in git).
- Paid path: Percy / Applitools / Chromatic — noise-tolerant diff, hosted review.
- Selenium: also plugin/SaaS territory. Visual tests are flake magnets (fonts, anti-aliasing, animation) — stabilize viewport, fonts, and data first.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## The interview trap

"Does Cypress support visual testing?" Accurate answer: **not built-in.** `cy.screenshot()` writes a PNG. Comparison, thresholding, and baseline management live in a plugin or a vendor. Playwright's `toHaveScreenshot()` is the contrast case — first-party, snapshot directory, threshold options. Selenium matches Cypress here: bring your own.

## Free plugin path

```bash
npm install -D cypress-image-snapshot
```

```js
// cypress/support/e2e.ts
import { addMatchImageSnapshotCommand } from 'cypress-image-snapshot/command';
addMatchImageSnapshotCommand({
  failureThreshold: 0.02,
  failureThresholdType: 'percent',
});

// spec
cy.visit('/payroll/summary');
cy.get('[data-cy=summary-cards]').matchImageSnapshot('payroll-summary-cards');
```

First run writes a baseline (commit it). Later runs fail when pixels move beyond the threshold. Same git-baseline discipline as Playwright screenshots.

## Paid SaaS path

Percy, Applitools, Chromatic (for component-centric UIs) add: hosted baselines, PR comments with diffs, reviewers who are not engineers, and algorithms that ignore anti-aliasing / sub-pixel font noise that wrecks raw pixel diffs across CI machines vs laptops.

```js
cy.visit('/dashboard');
cy.percySnapshot('HRM dashboard — manager');
```

Worth paying once visual review is an organizational workflow, not once you have three pages.

## Why visual tests flake

- Animations and spinners — wait for idle, or disable motion in test env.
- Dynamic data (clock, "3 pending requests") — freeze time (`cy.clock`) and stub APIs.
- Fonts not loaded — wait on `document.fonts.ready` via `cy.document()`.
- Viewport and OS DPI differences — pin `viewportWidth/Height`; prefer Docker `cypress/browsers` for CI parity (11.2).

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

| | Cypress | Playwright | Selenium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capture | `cy.screenshot()` | `page.screenshot()` | `TakesScreenshot` |
| Compare | Plugin/SaaS only | Built-in snapshot matcher | Plugin/SaaS only |
| Component visual | CT + plugin/Chromatic | CT/screenshot | N/A |

Interview line: "Cypress has no built-in visual regression. I screenshot for artifacts; I compare with a plugin or Percy. Playwright is the one with a first-party matcher."

chapters.title: 9.7 Accessibility Testing (cypress-axe)
chapters.overviewText: cypress-axe injects Deque's axe-core into the page and fails the spec on violations via cy.checkA11y(). It is the same engine Playwright teams wrap (axe-playwright / @axe-core/playwright). Selenium also uses axe via language bindings. None of these replace keyboard testing or screen-reader judgment; they catch a cheap, repeatable slice (contrast, labels, duplicate ids).
chapters.why: HRM UIs are full of forms and tables — axe catches missing labels on leave dates before a WCAG audit does. Interviewers like that you know inject-then-check order and that failures are axe violations, not Cypress core.
chapters.when: After a page reaches a stable, meaningful state (dashboard loaded, form open, modal visible). Not in beforeEach against a blank visit.

practical.scenario: You must gate the Leave Request modal against axe serious/critical issues, ignoring a known color-contrast ticket on the banner.
practical.pass: You cy.injectAxe() after the modal is open, then cy.checkA11y with a context selector and rules/impact filter. You do not skip axe because 'QA will test a11y later.'
practical.fail: You call checkA11y before injectAxe, or you treat axe as a full WCAG certification.

chapters.customSummary:
- cypress-axe wraps axe-core: cy.injectAxe() then cy.checkA11y().
- inject after the DOM you care about exists; check can be scoped to a selector.
- Default: violations fail the test; a callback can log-without-fail during a known-debt burn-down.
- Same engine as Playwright/Selenium axe integrations — tool choice is wiring, not rules.
- Complements, does not replace, keyboard and AT testing.

chapters.title: 9.8 Parallelization & Sharding
chapters.overviewText: In Cypress, 'parallel' means multiple machines (or multiple OS processes), each running one browser against a subset of spec files — not one Cypress process juggling Chrome and Firefox, and not one process with many browser contexts like Playwright workers. Cloud --parallel assigns specs using historical timings. Free options: cypress-parallel on one host, or a CI matrix that shards --spec lists by hand.
chapters.why: Misunderstanding this word designs a broken CI: people set --browser chrome,firefox and expect concurrency, or they buy Cloud when a matrix of three GitHub runners would do. Interviewers listen for 'machines, not browsers.'
chapters.when: When the suite exceeds ~10 minutes, when you add a second CI job, or when someone asks for 'parallel browsers.'

practical.scenario: The HRM suite is 40 minutes on one GitHub runner. Leadership wants 10-minute feedback on pull requests.
practical.pass: You split specs across N machines (Cloud --parallel or a matrix with spec globs). Each job still uses one browser. Chrome vs Firefox is additional jobs, not extra parallelism inside one job.
practical.fail: You pass multiple browsers to one cypress run and expect them to run at the same time, or you confuse Playwright worker processes with Cypress Cloud orchestration.

chapters.customSummary:
- Parallel = many machines/processes × one browser × a shard of specs — never many browsers inside one Cypress run.
- Cypress Cloud --record --parallel: smart historical load-balancing (paid).
- Free: cypress-parallel (one machine, many processes) or CI matrix + --spec globs (naive split).
- Playwright: workers on one machine + shard=1/N; Selenium Grid: many nodes. Different knobs, same goal (wall clock).
- Firefox+Chrome coverage is extra full-suite runs, multiplied by shard count.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Say the sentence out loud

"Cypress parallelization is spec-file sharding across machines, each machine running a single browser." If you cannot say that, do not draw the CI diagram yet.

One `cypress run --browser chrome` process = one browser. Two browsers = two invocations (or two jobs). Playwright can start N workers (browser contexts) in one machine more naturally; Cypress's unit of distribution is the **spec file**.

## Paid: Cypress Cloud

```bash
npx cypress run --record --key "$CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY" --parallel --ci-build-id "$GITHUB_RUN_ID"
```

All machines share a build id. Cloud hands the next spec to a free machine based on **historical duration**, so a 4-minute payroll spec does not land on the same shard as three other slow specs. That orchestration is what you pay for (Part 11.3). Without Cloud, you can still run many machines — you just split specs yourself.

## Free on one machine: cypress-parallel

Spawns several Cypress processes on one runner, each with a subset of specs. Bounded by that runner's CPU/RAM. Real speedup for a beefy self-hosted runner; limited on a small GitHub-hosted box.

## Free across machines: CI matrix (naive shard)

```yaml
strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    spec: ['cypress/e2e/leave/**', 'cypress/e2e/payroll/**', 'cypress/e2e/admin/**']
steps:
  - uses: cypress-io/github-action@v6
    with:
      browser: chrome
      spec: ${{ matrix.spec }}
```

Three machines, three folders. If leave is 5 minutes and payroll is 25, you wait 25. Cloud's balancer exists to fix that imbalance.

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

| Knob | Cypress | Playwright | Selenium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit of split | spec files | tests/workers + shard | tests across Grid nodes |
| One process, many browsers | No | Projects/matrix, still separate launches | Grid |
| Smart historical balance | Cloud paid | mostly DIY / third party | Grid labs / vendors |
| Multi-browser | extra jobs | extra projects/jobs | extra capabilities |

Interview line: "Parallel in Cypress means more machines sharding specs, each with one browser. It does not mean one run drives Chrome and Firefox together."

chapters.title: 9.9 Cross-Browser & Cross-Device Testing
chapters.overviewText: Cypress officially drives Chromium-family browsers (Chrome, Edge, Electron) and Firefox from local installs. WebKit — Safari's engine — has never had first-class official support. Device coverage is viewport emulation (cy.viewport / config), not real iPhones. Playwright includes WebKit natively; Selenium can drive SafariDriver on macOS. Real phones still want Appium or a vendor device cloud.
chapters.why: If Bizlevate's executives live in Safari, a Cypress-only matrix will not see WebKit layout bugs. Saying 'we test mobile' because you set iphone-x viewport is how teams ship broken iOS chrome.
chapters.when: When defining the CI browser matrix, when a bug is Safari-only, and when a ticket says 'mobile testing' (then read 9.17).

practical.scenario: You must propose a browser/device matrix for HRM: most employees on Chrome, finance on Safari, some on company iPhones.
practical.pass: You run Cypress on Chrome and Firefox in CI, state that WebKit is not first-class so Safari risk is Playwright or Sauce/LambdaTest Safari, and you treat cy.viewport as responsive-web only.
practical.fail: You add --browser webkit as if it were Playwright, or you call viewport iphone-x 'real device testing.'

chapters.customSummary:
- Official: Electron (bundled), Chrome, Edge, Firefox. No first-class WebKit/Safari.
- --browser selects one browser per run; matrix = multiple runs/jobs (see 9.8).
- cy.viewport / config viewportWidth+Height emulate size, not iOS WebKit or touch chrome.
- Playwright: Chromium + Firefox + WebKit first-class. Selenium: SafariDriver possible.
- Real devices: vendor cloud or Appium (native); Cypress is not a device lab.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## What Cypress will actually launch

```bash
npx cypress run --browser chrome
npx cypress run --browser edge
npx cypress run --browser firefox
npx cypress run --browser electron   # bundled default
```

Chrome/Edge/Firefox must be installed (or provided by `cypress/browsers` images, 11.2). Electron ships inside the npm package — that is why tutorials "just work" and why Electron-only CI misses Firefox bugs.

**WebKit:** experimental community runners have existed; they are not something you stake payroll-critical Safari coverage on. Playwright's `webkit` browser is the honest answer for first-class Safari-engine tests.

## Viewport is not a device

```js
cy.viewport('iphone-x');
cy.viewport(390, 844);
```

This resizes the iframe. It does not install iOS, does not use WebKit, does not fire real touch (there is `cypress-real-events` for closer pointer events — still desktop Chrome). Use it to catch CSS that collapses the leave calendar at 375px.

## A sane Bizlevate matrix

1. **PR gate:** Cypress Chrome headless (fast, majority users).
2. **Nightly:** Cypress Firefox + Chrome, same specs.
3. **Safari/WebKit critical journeys:** Playwright WebKit or a cloud Safari browser — *named as a different job*, not a Cypress flag you wish existed.
4. **Responsive:** a handful of specs with `cy.viewport` at mobile width.
5. **Native app:** Appium, if it exists (9.17).

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

Playwright's project matrix (`chromium`, `firefox`, `webkit`, pixel 5 viewport) is one config file. Selenium + Sauce Labs can request iPhone Safari capabilities Cypress cannot originate. Cypress wins DX on Chromium; it loses the "one tool, all engines" story.

Interview line: "Cypress has no first-class WebKit. I emulate devices with viewports. Safari-engine coverage is Playwright or a cloud browser, not a Cypress checkbox."

chapters.title: 9.10 Localization / i18n Testing
chapters.overviewText: i18n tests fail for the wrong reason when they assert English copy that marketing will change. Prefer stable locators (data-cy), assert translation keys or lang-specific fixtures, and control locale via URL, cookie, header, or app setting — not by hoping the CI machine is en-US. Playwright can set locale/timezone on a context at launch; Cypress sets the browser you launched and then drives the app's own i18n switch.
chapters.why: Bizlevate HRM ships English and Nepali (or Spanish) for leave types and payroll labels. A suite that `contains('Submit leave')` breaks on the Nepali build even when the feature works.
chapters.when: When adding a second language, when CI agents have unexpected OS locales, or when dates/currency formats differ (en-US 9/16/2026 vs en-GB 16/09/2026).

practical.scenario: Leave submit must work in en and ne-NP: same data-cy, different visible strings from fixtures.
practical.pass: You switch locale the way the app does (query, cookie, user profile), load strings from a fixture, and assert with data-cy plus fixture text — not hardcoded English only.
practical.fail: You assert cy.contains('Submit') in every spec and never set the app language.

chapters.customSummary:
- Do not couple specs to English marketing copy; use data-cy and fixture strings.
- Drive locale through the product (profile, ?lang=, cookie), then cy.visit.
- Dates, currency, and collation flake under OS locale — pin TZ and format in assertions.
- Playwright: browser.newContext({ locale, timezoneId }). Cypress: no equivalent context factory; control the app and the OS/container.
- Selenium: similar to Cypress — capabilities/chrome options, then the app.

chapters.title: 9.11 UI Mode
chapters.overviewText: Cypress UI Mode is the modern Cypress App experience around cypress open: launchpad, spec list that persists, run history across sessions, and the two-pane Command Log + app preview. It is the local interactive product. Playwright's npx playwright test --ui is a different program (trace-like timeline, watch mode, locator picker) — do not use the same words as if they were one feature.
chapters.why: Junior engineers search for Playwright's UI Mode flags inside Cypress and conclude Cypress 'has no UI.' The GUI is the whole Cypress bet; knowing the newer App vs classic runner vs Playwright --ui prevents that confusion.
chapters.when: Daily local development, debugging a failed spec visually, and when someone coming from Playwright asks 'where's UI Mode?'

practical.scenario: A leave spec failed last night. You want to re-run just that spec, inspect the DOM at the failed command, and see whether it failed the previous local run too.
practical.pass: You npx cypress open (E2E, Chrome), use the spec list + Command Log time-travel, and use run history if the App version provides it. You do not look for playwright test --ui.
practical.fail: You try npx cypress test --ui or expect a Playwright-style trace timeline in the open GUI.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cypress UI = cypress open / Cypress App (launchpad, spec list, Command Log, time-travel).
- Newer App builds add persistent run history and richer spec navigation — that is 'UI Mode' in this manual.
- Playwright --ui is watch mode + timeline; not available as a Cypress clone.
- cypress run is headless CI; headed CI is --headed, still not the App.
- Selenium has no equivalent first-party GUI runner.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## What you actually launch

```bash
npx cypress open          # Cypress App / UI
npx cypress run           # headless (CI default)
npx cypress run --headed  # CI-style run but visible browser, no App sidebar
```

`cypress open` is the product: pick E2E vs Component, pick browser, pick spec. The window is split — Command Log left, the live HRM iframe right. Hover a log line to time-travel the DOM (Part 0.7). That live loop is why frontend teams tolerate Cypress's architectural limits.

## What "UI Mode" means here

Newer Cypress App versions keep:

- a spec sidebar that does not vanish when a run ends
- run history so you can see "did `leave-submit.cy.ts` fail last time *on this machine*"
- search/filter across a large `cypress/e2e` tree

Treat that as Cypress **UI Mode**: the App behaving more like an IDE for tests. It is still not Playwright's UI Mode.

## Playwright UI Mode (so you can contrast)

`npx playwright test --ui` opens a runner with watch mode, a timeline of actions, pick-locator, and often a path into traces. Post-mortem for CI is still `trace.zip` (9.12). Cypress's interactive story is live snapshots; Playwright's is live inspector **plus** a portable trace file.

## Selenium

No first-party equivalent. People glue Teswell / vendor IDEs / IDE breakpoints on JUnit. Do not compare Cypress App to "Selenium IDE" record-and-playback as if they were the same generation of tool.

Interview line: "Cypress UI Mode is `cypress open` — live Command Log and time-travel. Playwright's `--ui` is a different runner. Cypress has no Trace Viewer in that window."

chapters.title: 9.12 Trace Viewer & Post-Mortem Debugging
chapters.overviewText: Cypress has no Trace Viewer and no trace.zip. Post-mortem on CI is videos, screenshots, the terminal error, Cypress Cloud Test Replay / Debug if you pay, and whatever you log with cy.task. Playwright records a zip you open with playwright show-trace. Do not tell a team to 'open the Cypress trace' — that sentence is a category error.
chapters.why: CI-only failures are the whole point of post-mortem tooling. Importing Playwright's mental model into Cypress Cloud sales calls — or worse, into a root-cause meeting — wastes hours.
chapters.when: When a spec fails on GitHub Actions but passes on your laptop, and whenever someone asks where the Cypress equivalent of Trace Viewer is.

practical.scenario: leave-approve.cy.ts failed on CI at cy.get('[data-cy=approve]'). You were not watching. You need to see DOM + network at that step.
practical.pass: You collect screenshot/video artifacts (11.8), use Cloud Test Replay if the project records, and use cy.task logs. You explicitly say there is no trace.zip / Trace Viewer in open-source Cypress.
practical.fail: You look for a traces/ folder or run npx cypress show-trace.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cypress OSS: no Trace Viewer, no trace.zip, no playwright show-trace equivalent.
- Local interactive: Command Log time-travel (not portable to CI).
- CI post-mortem: screenshots, videos (video defaulted to false in Cypress 13+), stdout, cy.task logs.
- Closest paid analog: Cypress Cloud Test Replay / Debug — not a zip you open offline.
- Playwright: portable trace zip. Selenium: vendor recordings or raw logs.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Two debugging times

**While you watch** (`cypress open`): click the failed command, inspect the restored DOM, read the intercept. That is time-travel. It requires the App. It does not produce a file for Slack.

**After CI already died:** you need artifacts that *survived the machine*. Cypress's open-source answers are:

- PNG via `screenshotOnRunFailure` (still true)
- MP4 via `video: true` (Cypress 13 changed the default to **false** — set it if you want videos)
- the Mocha error + any `cy.task('log', ...)` lines in the job log

There is **no** `playwright show-trace trace.zip` analog in `npm install cypress`.

## Cypress Cloud Debug / Test Replay

Paid Cloud can reconstruct a replay of the recorded run (DOM snapshots, console, network) in the dashboard. That is the closest *experience* to Trace Viewer, with two differences you must name:

1. It is **hosted and licensed**, not a zip in the repo.
2. It is not the Playwright Trace Viewer UI; do not teach Cloud as "Cypress Trace Viewer."

If the org will not pay, your post-mortem design is artifacts + logging (11.7, 11.8), not wishful tracing.

## Make CI failures diagnosable without Cloud

```js
// noisy but honest
afterEach(function () {
  if (this.currentTest.state === 'failed') {
    cy.task('log', {
      title: this.currentTest.title,
      error: this.currentTest.err?.message,
    });
  }
});
```

Prefer `cy.task` over `cy.log` for CI: `cy.log` is a Command Log pretty-print; many CI terminals never show it (11.7).

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

| | Cypress | Playwright | Selenium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Live | App time-travel | Inspector / UI Mode | IDE debugger |
| Portable post-mortem | video/screenshot; Cloud Replay (paid) | **trace.zip** | vendor video / logs |
| Open offline | video player | `show-trace` | depends |

Interview line: "Cypress has no Trace Viewer. OSS post-mortem is screenshots/videos plus logs. Cloud Debug/Test Replay is the paid cousin of Playwright's zip, not the same artifact."

chapters.title: 9.13 Flaky Test Management
chapters.overviewText: A flaky test is one that fails without a product change. Cypress retries (Part 10.3) and Cloud flake charts can hide the fire — a test that passes on retry is still broken. Detect via history, quarantine with an owner, then fix root causes (timing, isolation, data, origin/tab workarounds). Playwright's retries and pytest-rerunfailures have the same moral hazard.
chapters.why: Once Bizlevate's team says 'just re-run CI,' the suite has stopped being a gate. Flake management is process plus architecture, not a retries: 2 config flex.
chapters.when: When a spec is red then green on the same commit, when Cloud marks a test flaky, or when you are tempted to raise retries to make the PR green.

practical.scenario: leave-balance.cy.ts fails ~1 in 8 on CI, always passes locally. Retries are set to 2 so PRs merge.
practical.pass: You treat retries as a detector, quarantine or fix the spec (session, intercept, clock, isolation), and you do not raise retries to hide it.
practical.fail: You set retries: 5 and delete the Slack alert.

chapters.customSummary:
- Flake = intermittent fail without code change; retries hide it unless you still track retry-pass as a smell.
- Detect with history (Cloud analytics or CI logs), not one red run.
- Quarantine is temporary and owned — not a parking lot.
- Usual Cypress causes: hard waits, shared state, animations, origin/tab substitutes, CI vs local timing.
- Playwright/Selenium retries have the same trap. Fix the test or the app.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Definition and the retries trap

If the spec is green on the second attempt, Cypress (and GitHub's "re-run failed jobs") will show a green check. **The flake is still there.** Part 10.3 covers the `retries` config. This chapter is the policy: retries are a shock absorber, not a root-cause tool.

Cypress Cloud flake detection (paid) plots pass rate over time. Without Cloud, grep CI for "because the test retried" / Mocha retry output, or require a dashboard alternative (11.5).

## Causes that show up in HRM suites

1. **Time** — `cy.wait(2000)` instead of `cy.wait('@getLeave')` or `.should('be.visible')`.
2. **Isolation** — `testIsolation: false` leftover leave drafts; order-dependent specs.
3. **Data** — two jobs creating "Ava Sharma" unique-constraint collisions.
4. **Animation / overlay** — click hitting a toast that is exiting.
5. **Architecture substitutes** — SSO without a stable `cy.origin` block; PDF tab tests that sometimes race the download.
6. **Environment** — local SSD vs CI CPU; missing `TZ`; video encoding load.

## Process that actually works

- **Detect:** tag metrics; a test that retried is a ticket, not a win.
- **Quarantine:** `it.skip` or grep-plugin tag `@flake` excluded from the merge gate (10.1), with an assignee and a date.
- **Fix:** intercept, `cy.session`, clock, unique test data, fewer visits.
- **Re-enable:** history goes back to 100% or the test is deleted.

Playwright Trace Viewer makes flake *easier to inspect* after the fact. Cypress OSS needs video + time-travel locally + Cloud Replay if you have it (9.12). The process is the same.

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

All three ecosystems invented retries because UI is timing-sensitive. None of them make retries a virtue. Selenium Grid even more so (session drops). Senior answer: "I use retries to *surface* flake in reports, then I fix isolation or waiting. I do not ship retries as the fix."

Interview line: "Retries hide flake. I track retry-passes as failures of the suite's trust, quarantine with an owner, and fix waits/data/isolation."

chapters.title: 9.14 Data-Driven / Looped Tests
chapters.overviewText: Data-driven Cypress means generating it() blocks from an array or fixture — each row is its own test title, screenshot, and retry — not a for-loop of cy.get inside one it(). Mocha/Cypress collect tests synchronously; if you cy.fixture inside it() and loop there, you get one test and opaque failures. Playwright's for (const data of list) test() pattern is the same idea with different syntax.
chapters.why: Leave types, roles, and payroll countries explode combinatorially. One looped it() that fails on row 6 reports as a single failed test named 'validates leave types'.
chapters.when: When the same journey must run for many roles, locales, or CSV rows. Not when the rows are steps of one user journey (those stay one it).

practical.scenario: You must assert the leave-type dropdown contains Annual, Sick, Bereavement, Unpaid for both admin and employee fixtures.
practical.pass: You load a static fixture/array at spec top level (or require JSON) and forEach to emit separate it() titles. Failure names the row.
practical.fail: You nest cy.fixture().then(rows => rows.forEach(... cy.get ...)) inside a single it() and call it data-driven.

chapters.customSummary:
- Generate it() from a synchronous array/require(fixture), not a for-loop of commands inside one test.
- Each row = one test name, one retry, one screenshot.
- cy.fixture is async — too late to register tests if you call it inside it().
- Playwright: loop calling test(); Selenium: TestNG DataProvider / pytest parametrize.
- Keep combinatorial explosion in CT (9.5) when it is prop-level, not full E2E.

chapters.title: 9.15 cy.screenshot() API
chapters.overviewText: cy.screenshot() captures the current app iframe (or an element, or the runner) to cypress/screenshots. It is an artifact API — naming, capture, blackout, overwrite, onAfterScreenshot — not visual regression. Automatic failure screenshots are configured separately (screenshotOnRunFailure). Playwright splits page.screenshot vs expect().toHaveScreenshot; Cypress puts capture here and comparison in plugins (9.6).
chapters.why: You will use this in CI artifacts, in docs, and when blacking out PII on payroll screens before a PNG leaves the runner. Confusing it with matchImageSnapshot causes false confidence.
chapters.when: On failure (automatic), at explicit checkpoints, and when a report needs a still. Not as your visual-diff strategy.

practical.scenario: Payroll run confirmation shows bank account numbers. You need a screenshot for the failure report with the account blacked out.
practical.pass: You cy.get(card).screenshot({ blackout: ['[data-cy=iban]'] }) and know this does not compare to a baseline.
practical.fail: You use cy.screenshot() as a visual assertion, or you screenshot the whole runner including the Command Log when you meant the app only.

chapters.customSummary:
- cy.screenshot() writes PNG artifacts; it does not diff.
- Capture modes: fullPage, viewport, runner, or element via cy.get().screenshot().
- blackout hides secrets; overwrite avoids timestamp clutter.
- Failure screenshots: screenshotOnRunFailure (distinct from calling the command).
- Playwright: screenshot vs toHaveScreenshot are different APIs — Cypress only ships the first.

chapters.title: 9.16 Migrating from Protractor/Selenium to Cypress
chapters.overviewText: Protractor is dead (Angular dropped it); Selenium remains a valid external-driver stack. Migration is not findElement → cy.get line substitution. You move from awaited WebDriver calls and window handles to a command queue, from multi-tab/SOP freedom to cy.origin and no switchToTab, and from Java/Python to JS/TS. Rewrite critical journeys; do not transpile tests.
chapters.why: Many HRM estates still have Protractor or TestNG+Selenium. Interviewers ask how you would migrate without a six-month freeze. The answer is architecture mapping plus a thin parallel run, not a regex.
chapters.when: When a team is stuck on Protractor, when Selenium tests are unmaintainable, or when a JS frontend team wants ownership of E2E.

practical.scenario: Bizlevate has 200 Protractor specs (including Okta and a PDF tab) and wants Cypress for the React rewrite.
practical.pass: You rewrite leave/payroll happy paths in Cypress with data-cy, map SSO to cy.origin, move PDF-tab cases to request/href or keep them in Selenium/Playwright, and you do not mechanically rewrite browser.switchTo().
practical.fail: You search-replace element(by.css) with cy.get and ship it, including switchTo().window.

chapters.customSummary:
- Protractor is discontinued — migrate; do not 'upgrade Protractor.'
- Selenium→Cypress is an execution-model change (external driver → in-page queue), not an API rename.
- No 1:1 for window handles, implicit waits, or Java DataProviders (see 9.14).
- Keep Playwright/Selenium for WebKit/multi-tab if those paths are critical.
- Parallel run + rewrite highest-value journeys; kill the old suite in slices.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Protractor is not "old Cypress"

Protractor wrapped WebDriver + Angular-specific waiting. It died with Angular's official support. Cypress is not its successor by vendor; it is a different architecture that *also* lives in JS. Treat Protractor migration as a green-field Cypress suite informed by the old scenarios, not as a port.

## Mechanical maps that *do* help

| Legacy | Cypress |
|---|---|
| `element(by.css('[data-cy=x]'))` | `cy.get('[data-cy=x]')` |
| `browser.get(url)` | `cy.visit(url)` |
| `ExpectedConditions.visibilityOf` | `.should('be.visible')` (retry-ability) |
| `browser.sleep(2000)` | delete; wait on UI or `@alias` |
| TestNG DataProvider | generated `it()` (9.14) |
| `browser.switchTo().frame` | `cy.get(iframe).its('0.contentDocument.body')` then `cy.wrap` — or `cy.origin` if the iframe is another origin |
| `switchTo().window` | **no equivalent** — 9.3 |
| `driver.get('https://okta...')` after app | `cy.origin` — 9.1 |

## Maps that will hurt you

- **Implicit waits + explicit waits stacked** → Cypress retry-ability already waits; adding `cy.wait(5000)` re-imports Selenium slowness.
- **Page objects that return WebElements** → return chainables or use app actions (Part 8).
- **`async/await` around every get** → Cypress commands are not Promises (Part 0.3). `await cy.get()` is a bug.
- **Keeping Java** — Cypress is JS/TS only. A Java Selenium org is often a better Playwright-Java or stay-Selenium decision than a language rewrite.

## Suggested migration slices for Bizlevate

1. Install Cypress, agree `data-cy` on the React rewrite.
2. Port **login + dashboard** (session, not UI login every test).
3. Port **leave submit/approve** — highest regression cost.
4. SSO: write `cy.origin` once, wrap with `cy.session`.
5. PDF/new-tab: do not port `switchTo`; use 9.3 or leave those few tests in Selenium/Playwright.
6. Turn off the equivalent Protractor specs as each slice goes green in CI (Part 11).

## Versus Playwright as the destination

If the remaining Selenium suite is Python, multi-tab heavy, or Safari-critical, Playwright may be the better *target* than Cypress. Cypress is the better target when the owners are frontend engineers and CT matters (9.5). Tool choice is who maintains the tests.

Interview line: "I don't regex Protractor into Cypress. I rewrite journeys onto the command queue, map SSO to `cy.origin`, and I refuse to port `switchTo().window`."

chapters.title: 9.17 Mobile Testing — Real Limitations
chapters.overviewText: Cypress can emulate a mobile viewport and, with plugins, closer pointer events. It cannot automate a compiled iOS/Android HRM app from the store — that is Appium (or Detox/Espresso/XCUITest). It also cannot honestly claim Safari/iOS web coverage because there is no first-class WebKit. 'We test mobile with Cypress' only means 'responsive web in a skinny Chromium iframe' unless you add other tools.
chapters.why: Product will ask why the native app has no Cypress tests after a successful web rollout. The precise boundary protects you from promising Appium work in Cypress, and it is an interview staple.
chapters.when: When the roadmap includes an iOS app, when a bug is 'only on my iPhone,' and when designing the test pyramid for a 'mobile-first' HRM.

practical.scenario: Bizlevate plans a native iOS app for leave submit plus the existing responsive web app. Leadership asks to 'just point Cypress at iOS.'
practical.pass: You keep Cypress for responsive web (viewport, maybe a cloud mobile Chrome), and you name Appium (or vendor device cloud with real Safari) for native and real iOS web. You do not say Cypress runs in the App Store binary.
practical.fail: You set cy.viewport('iphone-x') and report mobile native coverage as done.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cypress = web in a browser you launched. Viewport ≠ iPhone.
- No first-class WebKit ⇒ weak iOS Safari story (9.9).
- Native store apps: Appium (or platform-native frameworks), not Cypress.
- Playwright: better iOS-web via WebKit, still not native Appium.
- Real devices: vendor labs (BrowserStack/Sauce) or Appium grid.
